options: How soon should this be fixed?
How much impact does the defect have on the system or its users?
Who should fix the defect?
How many times was the defect reproduced?
questions.explanation: Severity measures impact. 'How soon' is priority, which depends on business context. Assignee and reproduction count are separate fields.

questions.prompt: In most teams the tester proposes severity, while the product owner or a triage meeting decides priority.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Testers observe the technical impact, so they usually propose severity. Priority is a business scheduling decision, so the product owner or triage group owns it.

questions.prompt: A checkout page crashes for every user when they click Pay. Which rating is most appropriate?
options: Low severity, low priority
High severity, low priority
High severity, high priority
Low severity, high priority
questions.explanation: Nobody can buy anything: the impact is critical and the business needs it fixed immediately. The other quadrants understate either impact or urgency.

questions.prompt: A spelling mistake appears in the legal terms shown on the payment page. Legal says the wrong word changes the meaning of a refund clause, and the release goes out tomorrow. What is the best rating?
options: Low severity, low priority: it is only a typo
Low severity, high priority: functional impact is small but it must be fixed before release
High severity, low priority: the text is legally important but can wait
It should not be logged; text is the content team's job
questions.explanation: The software still works, so functional severity is low, but the business and legal consequence makes it urgent. Calling it 'only a typo' ignores context; not logging it loses the record.

questions.prompt: Which changes could legitimately lower a defect's priority while its severity stays the same? Select all that apply.
options: A reliable workaround is published to affected users
The feature it affects is switched off by a feature flag for this release
The developer finds the fix difficult
The affected customer segment turns out to be one internal test account
questions.explanation: Workarounds, disabling the feature and a tiny affected audience all reduce urgency. The difficulty of the fix affects effort and scheduling discussions, but by itself it does not make the defect less urgent for users.

questions.prompt: Why do teams keep severity and priority as two separate fields instead of one 'importance' field?
options: Because Jira requires two fields
Because all four combinations occur in practice, and one field would hide either impact or urgency
Because severity is only used for reports to management
Because priority is set automatically from severity
questions.explanation: High-severity/low-priority and low-severity/high-priority defects are real. A single field forces you to lose one of the two pieces of information. Priority is not derived mechanically from severity.

questions.prompt: A team's backlog shows 140 open defects, all marked 'Critical'. Triage has stopped being useful. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Developers are too slow
There are no written definitions with examples for each severity level, so testers rate everything as high
The defect tool is misconfigured
Testers should stop rating severity at all
questions.explanation: Severity inflation happens when levels lack agreed definitions. The fix is a written scale with examples and calibration, not removing the field or blaming developers.

questions.prompt: A banking app's monthly statement PDF shows the wrong closing balance for accounts with more than 999 transactions in a month. About 30 business customers are affected; statements are generated on the 1st, which is 3 weeks away; a manual corrected statement can be produced by operations. How should you rate and act?
options: Low severity, low priority; close as an edge case
High severity (incorrect financial data); priority high enough to fix before the next run on the 1st, with operations' manual workaround as a fallback
Low severity, high priority because only 30 customers are affected
High severity, highest priority: stop all other work and hotfix tonight
questions.explanation: Wrong financial figures are high impact regardless of how many accounts are affected. The 3-week window and a workaround mean it needs scheduling before the next run, not an emergency hotfix tonight, and certainly not closing.

questions.prompt: Two weeks ago a defect was rated High severity, Low priority because the affected admin report was unused. Marketing now plans to send that report to all partners next Monday. What should happen to the defect?
options: Nothing; ratings are fixed once triaged
Re-raise it at triage so priority is re-evaluated in the new context; severity stays the same
Raise its severity to Critical so it gets attention
Close it and open a new defect
questions.explanation: Priority depends on context and should be re-evaluated when context changes. Severity describes impact, which has not changed, so inflating it would distort the data. Duplicating the defect loses history.
